events.title: The London Carthusian martyrs
events.shortBlurb: The first blood of the English Reformation was shed at Tyburn when three monastic priors refused the royal supremacy…
body: On 4 May 1535, at Tyburn outside London, the first blood of Henry VIII's Reformation was shed: John Houghton, prior of the London Charterhouse, with two fellow Carthusian priors, Robert Lawrence of Beauvale and Augustine Webster of Axholme, and with them Richard Reynolds, a Bridgettine of Syon Abbey, and John Haile, a secular priest.

Their offence was refusal of the Oath of Supremacy, by which the Act of 1534 made the king supreme head of the Church in England. Tried at Westminster and condemned as traitors, they were hanged in their religious habits, cut down alive, and disemboweled; Houghton suffered first, and one of his quarters was nailed over the gate of his own Charterhouse.

Three more of the London community suffered at Tyburn that June, and nine died in prison in 1537. The martyrs of 4 May were beatified under Leo XIII and numbered among the Forty Martyrs of England and Wales canonized by Paul VI on 25 October 1970.
